The Neon flying squid (Ommastrephes bartramii) exhibits a striking sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, a pattern that emerges from distinct growth trajectories and reproductive schedules that have been documented through extensive field surveys and laboratory analyses. Field studies based on systematic trawl collections across the central North Pacific have consistently demonstrated that females attain a maximum mantle length at death of 90.0 centimeters [Li = 90.0 centimeters], a value that greatly exceeds that of males and ranks among the largest recorded within the family Ommastrephidae. In contrast, male conspecifics rarely surpass a mantle length at death of 45.0 centimeters [Li = 45.0 centimeters], suggesting that divergent energetic demands and mortality risks fundamentally shape the adult body plan of each sex. This pronounced size disparity, with females reaching twice the mantle length of males, is one of the most prominent life-history features of the species and carries significant implications for reproductive output, foraging ecology, and vulnerability to predation throughout the adult stage.

Sexual maturation in Ommastrephes bartramii commences considerably earlier than the attainment of maximum body size, with the onset of puberty occurring at distinctly different mantle lengths for males and females, a pattern that reflects sex-specific selective pressures on growth and reproduction. For females, the transition to reproductive maturity is reached at a mantle length of 40.0 centimeters [Lp = 40.0 centimeters], based on histological analyses of gonad development in specimens collected from productive waters of the central North Pacific gyre. Males, following a faster developmental pace that aligns with their smaller ultimate size, typically undergo gonadal activation and attain puberty at a mantle length of 31.5 centimeters [Lp = 31.5 centimeters], approximately nine centimetres earlier than their female counterparts. This earlier maturation in males corresponds with their reduced somatic growth potential and suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive opportunity over continued expansion of body size, a common pattern among cephalopods with pronounced sexual dimorphism.

Reproductive investment in this pelagic squid is formidable, with females accumulating a substantial number of oocytes over their lifetime to maximize reproductive success under the challenging conditions of the open ocean. Under the thermal regime characteristic of the species' preferred habitat, specifically at a water temperature of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C], the cumulative reproductive output at the time of death has been estimated to be approximately 4 million eggs , based on thorough counts of mature oocytes in the oviducts and ovaries of recently spent females. This figure, derived from comprehensive fecundity studies, aligns with the high fecundity typical of many ommastrephid squids and reflects a life-history strategy that compensates for potentially high larval mortality through the production of numerous, small, and energetically inexpensive offspring that are released into the plankton.

At the very start of the life cycle, the wet weight at birth provides a critical baseline for understanding the species' early energetic requirements and the constraints imposed by small egg size in a pelagic environment. Based on a mean oocyte diameter of approximately 0.99 millimetres and the assumption of spherical geometry, the newly spawned egg has a wet weight of 0.00051 grams [Wwb = 0.00051 grams], an exceedingly minute initial mass that places Ommastrephes bartramii among the many cephalopods that produce large numbers of very small pelagic eggs. These diminutive eggs subsequently undergo a vulnerable planktonic phase characterized by high mortality from predation but potentially rapid growth when food resources and temperature conditions are favorable, allowing survivors to quickly outgrow their most susceptible size classes.

The maximum lifespan for female Neon flying squid has been established through detailed analyses of statolith daily increment counts, which serve as reliable age markers in cephalopods and allow precise estimation of longevity in wild-caught specimens. Individuals reared or living under conditions consistent with the species' typical thermal environment, specifically at a water temperature of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C], have a documented lifespan of approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days], a duration that corresponds to a classic one-year life cycle. This semelparous strategy is common among ommastrephid squids, where a single, intense reproductive episode at the end of the first year of life leads to rapid physiological senescence and death of the spawning individuals, completing the annual turnover that sustains the population.
